addressed_problems.content: The Lottery Pools method proposed in this paper uses a greedy, validation-guided search over a discrete set of candidate interpolation coefficients and subnetworks to improve the accuracy of lottery ticket subnetworks. The authors note that learning optimal interpolation coefficients and selecting subnetworks via gradient-based or joint optimization is possible but computationally expensive. The unresolved issue is whether such a gradient-based or joint optimization approach can yield further performance gains beyond the greedy search at a reasonable computational cost, and whether the additional cost is justified by the potential improvement.

The paper reports that experiments on ImageNet were run only once due to limited computational resources, meaning that the variability of Lottery Pools across multiple independent runs on this large-scale dataset has not been assessed. The unresolved empirical task is to establish the statistical significance and evaluate the variability of the performance gains of Lottery Pools over standard Lottery Tickets across multiple independent runs on ImageNet, which is necessary to confirm the reliability and generalizability of the method on large-scale benchmarks.

The paper evaluates Lottery Pools on VGG-16, ResNet-18, and ResNet-34, but does not test on substantially larger modern architectures such as transformers or very deep convolutional networks. The unresolved empirical task is to evaluate whether the interpolation benefits of Lottery Pools persist on substantially larger modern architectures, and to characterize the performance gains in those settings. This is important for understanding the scalability and practical applicability of the method to state-of-the-art models.

The paper demonstrates performance gains at various sparsity levels across multiple datasets, but does not characterize how the benefits of interpolation scale with model size, dataset complexity, number of IMP iterations, or sparsity regime. The unresolved empirical task is to systematically characterize the scaling behavior of Lottery Pools, including how the performance gains depend on these factors. This would help determine the regimes where the method is most beneficial and guide its application to new problems.

The paper empirically observes that rewinding is necessary for successful weight interpolation between lottery ticket subnetworks, and that adjacency in IMP iteration correlates with interpolation success. However, a precise theoretical characterization of when two IMP subnetworks are linearly mode-connected (i.e., can be interpolated without loss of accuracy) is not provided. The unresolved scientific question is to develop a theoretical understanding of the conditions for linear mode connectivity between sparse subnetworks identified by iterative magnitude pruning, including the roles of SGD noise, the rewinding point, and prediction diversity. Such a theory would explain the empirical observations and could guide the design of more effective interpolation strategies.

Deep neural networks achieve strong predictive performance but incur high computational and memory costs; sparsity via pruning is a leading approach to reduce model size while preserving accuracy. The Lottery Ticket (LTs) paradigm (iterative magnitude pruning, IMP) produces sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) that can be trained in isolation to match dense-network performance, but the standard IMP workflow is costly (many prune-and-retrain cycles) and, critically, discards intermediate subnetworks produced at earlier IMP iterations. This leaves two practical and scientific gaps. First, the byproduct subnetworks from IMP are underutilized: although ensemble methods can leverage multiple trained models to improve predictions, naïve ensemble increases inference cost linearly in the number of members and does not produce individually stronger sparse subnetworks. Second, it is unclear how to combine the multiple subnetworks produced by IMP to produce a single stronger subnetwork without additional training or extra inference cost; prior weight-averaging and interpolation techniques for dense models do not directly address: (a) maintaining the target sparsity after combination, (b) instability of linear connections when subnetworks are not rewound (i.e., when rewinding is not used), and (c) the choice of interpolation coefficients and which candidate subnetworks to combine. These limitations prevent reusing the computational effort already spent producing intermediate LTs, impede obtaining stronger sparse subnetworks at fixed sparsity and fixed inference cost, and leave open whether interpolation/averaging of IMP-produced subnetworks can yield robust in-distribution and out-of-distribution improvements without extra compute.

nodes.content: In the context of reusing IMP byproducts, researchers need a precise, operational definition of how two sparse subnetworks can be combined into a single candidate subnetwork while preserving sparsity. Prior dense-model averaging work gives averaging rules for dense parameters, but it is unclear how to form a self-contained interpolated sparse parameter vector and then restore the target sparsity without retraining. A concrete interpolation formula with an explicit post-interpolation pruning step is necessary to specify the operation that combines subnetworks and to enable empirical evaluation of whether such combinations can yield improved accuracy at fixed sparsity.

Practitioners require an operational method to exploit multiple IMP-produced subnetworks to obtain a single improved sparse subnetwork while preserving the original sparsity and without incurring extra training or inference cost. Prior ensemble approaches improve predictions only at the cost of multiple forward passes; naive averaging (fixed $\alpha=0.5$) can reduce sparsity and may not hit the best interpolation coefficient; exhaustive coefficient optimization or gradient-based learning of coefficients is computationally expensive and memory-intensive if all candidates are kept in memory. Therefore, a memory-frugal, validation-guided search that selects both candidate subnetworks and per-candidate interpolation coefficients, while pruning after each interpolation to enforce sparsity, is needed to make practical use of IMP byproducts.

The pre-contribution situation was that standard IMP outputs a single target-sparsity subnetwork while discarding earlier subnetworks, and there was no established, low-cost method to convert those multiple IMP byproducts into a single improved sparse subnetwork. Researchers needed a method that (a) preserves the target sparsity, (b) does not require retraining, and (c) provides quantitative evidence of improvement across architectures and datasets. Without such a method, practitioners could not reuse the computation of intermediate IMP iterations to derive stronger sparse models, and reported LTs performance remained the baseline for sparse-model accuracy at given sparsities.

Even when the goal is a high-accuracy dense model, intermediate IMP subnetworks represent distinct trained parameter configurations that are normally ignored after pruning. There was no low-cost procedure to merge the information contained in those subnetworks to strengthen the dense pre-trained model without further training. A method that combines IMP subnetworks into a stronger dense parameter vector while exploiting no extra training steps would allow practitioners to improve the dense baseline using only the outputs of a single IMP run.

Ensembles are known to improve OoD robustness, but naive ensembles of LTs increase inference cost and do not produce individually stronger sparse subnetworks. There was no method that both preserves single-model inference cost and transfers ensemble-like robustness benefits into a single sparse (or dense) model derived from IMP outputs. Practitioners thus lacked a way to transform multiple IMP checkpoints into a single model with enhanced OoD robustness at the same inference cost.

Existing weight-averaging baselines such as SWA and EMA average checkpoints using fixed coefficients or decay rules that were designed for dense-model trajectories; these baselines do not search per-pair interpolation coefficients and do not selectively exclude candidate checkpoints that degrade target-sparsity performance after pruning. As a result, prior averaging methods provided limited improvements for sparse LTs, particularly at high sparsity, leaving a performance gap for methods that combine multiple IMP outputs into a single robust sparse model.

Prior observations established that stability to SGD noise and linear mode connectivity influence whether two trained models can be linearly connected. For IMP-produced subnetworks, practitioners needed to know whether interpolation/averaging would be viable under standard LTs setups. If linear connections do not exist (e.g., when subnetworks are trained from initialization without rewinding), any attempt to average/interpolate could harm performance. A clear empirical characterization of the role of rewinding was therefore required to delimit when interpolation-based combination methods are applicable.

Combining subnetworks by interpolation can decrease effective sparsity if no pruning is applied; a search that ignores the target sparsity during intermediate steps may select candidates that look good before pruning but degrade sharply after pruning. Practitioners need a search policy that evaluates candidate interpolations at the target sparsity to avoid such selection errors; otherwise, the final pruned model may underperform.

A practical deployment of Lottery Pools must trade off search cost (memory and validation evaluations) against potential accuracy gains. Prior methods did not specify how many candidate checkpoints or interpolation coefficients are needed to realize most of the benefit. Empirical guidance about the marginal utility of adding candidates is necessary to design memory- and compute-aware workflows.

Ensembles of subnetworks achieve higher predictive performance and robustness but require multiple forward passes and proportional inference resources. To be useful in resource-constrained settings, a method is needed that delivers ensemble-like predictive gains without increasing inference cost. Demonstrating that a single Lottery Pools subnetwork matches the output ensemble's performance provides such a low-cost alternative.

A sparse interpolated subnetwork between two learned Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) subnetworks is defined by the linear interpolation
      $$
      \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter} = \alpha \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_1 + (1 - \alpha)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_2,
      $$
      where each $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i$ denotes a learned sparse subnetwork parameter vector (i.e., a dense parameter vector with zeros at pruned positions under a binary mask) and the interpolation coefficient $\alpha \in [0,1]$. After forming $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter}$, magnitude pruning is applied to remove the smallest-magnitude weights so that the resulting interpolated subnetwork attains the same sparsity as the higher sparsity of the two parent subnetworks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 defines the linear interpolation formula with post-interpolation magnitude pruning. This is a definitional/operational claim, not a factual assertion about the world. No load-bearing weak points were identified because there is no uncertain bridge: the formula is directly written and the post-pruning step is explicitly specified. H1 provides substantial evidence that the linear path between adjacent subnetworks is indeed a valley of low loss, giving mechanistic credit to the interpolation operation itself. The derivative supports the conclusion's built-in premise that the interpolated weights are a sensible object to evaluate. The combination of a precise, well-defined formula (which could fail if the linear path were not valid) and strong empirical validation of the underlying linear connectivity makes this a fully supported conclusion. The prior probability is set to 1 because the conclusion is essentially a definition that is shown to work, not a conjecture.

nodes.title: Interpolation of two learned Iterative Magnitude Pruning subnetworks

nodes.content: A practical algorithmic recipe, called Lottery Pools, constructs a stronger subnetwork from an Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP)-produced target subnetwork $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$ by (1) forming a Candidate Lottery Pool $\mathcal{S}_t=\{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t-1},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t+1},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t+2},\dots\}$ ordered by adjacency in IMP iterations; (2) defining a Candidate Coefficient Pool $\mathcal{S}_c=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$ with $\alpha_j\in(0,1)$; (3) greedily iterating over $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i\in\mathcal{S}_t$, selecting for each candidate the coefficient $\alpha_{best}=\arg\max_j \text{ValAcc}(\text{MagnitudePruning}(\alpha_j\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}+(1-\alpha_j)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i))$, forming $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}=\text{MagnitudePruning}(\alpha_{best}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}+(1-\alpha_{best})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i)$, and replacing $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ by $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}$ only if its validation accuracy $\text{ValAcc}$ does not decrease; and (4) repeating until all candidates are considered, yielding a final $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ that has the same sparsity as $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$. This procedure requires no additional network training and preserves single-model inference cost ($\mathcal{O}(1)$) relative to a single subnetwork.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 describes the full algorithmic recipe (Lottery Pools). The dominant risk is P1: the validation set-based greedy search may overfit to a 5,000-image hold-out split, inflating the claimed improvements. P10 adds a secondary risk: the sequential accumulation of interpolations could drift from the target basin, making the final subnetwork sensitive to candidate ordering. Both premises target the mechanism that produces the "stronger subnetwork." On the credit side, H2 (memory-friendly design) underwrites the feasibility of the recipe as O(1) memory overhead, which is a key component of the conclusion's claim of no extra cost. H1 supports the linear connectivity assumption used in the recipe, but that credit is indirect (it supports the interpolation primitive). H5 (sensitivity analysis) and H4 (prune-during ablation) are specific to subsequent conclusions (C9, C8). For C2 itself, the load-bearing protection comes only from H2; the overfitting risk (P1) is unprotected by any highlight that specifically preempts validation overfitting. Repeated evaluations on a small held-out set without cross-validation is a standard concern and the paper does not address it (e.g., by using a separate validation set or nested cross-validation). The overall credibility is moderate: the recipe is clearly defined and likely to produce gains in many settings, but the validation-set overfitting risk tempers the strength of the quantitative improvements reported from that search.

nodes.title: Lottery Pools: greedy interpolation recipe producing a stronger subnetwork at fixed sparsity without extra training or inference cost

nodes.content: Applying Lottery Pools (Interpolation) to Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP)-produced subnetworks yields consistent increases in test accuracy of the resulting sparse subnetworks across architectures (VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34) and datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) at multiple sparsity levels. Quantitatively, on CIFAR-100 Lottery Pools (Interpolation) improves over original Lottery Tickets (LTs) by up to 1.88 percentage points with VGG-16 and up to 1.72 percentage points with ResNet-18; on CIFAR-10 it yields up to 0.93 percentage points (VGG-16) and 1.05 percentage points (ResNet-18); on ImageNet it yields up to 0.55 (ResNet-18) and 0.63 (ResNet-34) percentage point improvements for sparse LTs.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 claims consistent in-distribution accuracy gains across architectures and datasets. The load-bearing uncertainties are P2 (only 3 runs on CIFAR, insufficient for statistical significance of many of the reported gains) and P3 (single-run ImageNet results provide no error bar). These operate on the quantitative layer: if the gains are not statistically reliable, the claim of "consistent increase" is unsupported for many configurations. On the CIFAR side, H8 (standard deviations reported) provides some credit by showing low variability, but it does not fully compensate for the very small sample size (3) because t-based confidence intervals remain wide. On the ImageNet side, H7 (consistent direction across two architectures) provides weak credit — it shows qualitative consistency but cannot quantify the uncertainty. The dominant risk is P2, which is directly about the statistical foundation of the quantitative gains. Without a formal statistical test or more runs, the conclusion's quantitative precision is fragile. The prior probability reflects that the method likely does improve accuracy (based on the consistent direction and small standard errors), but the evidence is not strong enough to confidently claim that the improvements are uniformly positive across all tested configurations.

nodes.title: Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields in-distribution accuracy gains across architectures and datasets

nodes.content: Averaging the set of learned Lottery Tickets (LTs) subnetworks back into the pre-trained dense network (via the Lottery Pools interpolation procedure) can produce a dense network with higher accuracy than the original pre-trained dense model. Empirically, on CIFAR-100 the resulting dense network exceeds the original dense ResNet-18 by up to 2.22 percentage points and the original dense VGG-16 by up to 1.69 percentage points; on ImageNet the constructed denser networks show improvements of up to 0.71 (ResNet-18) and 0.76 (ResNet-34) percentage points.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 claims that averaging LTs back into the dense pre-trained network (via the same interpolation procedure) produces stronger dense networks. This claim depends on the same empirical evidence as Conclusion 3 (the dense column in Tables 8-10) and is subject to identical statistical limitations (P2, P3). The protective highlights are also the same: H7 (ImageNet consistency) and H8 (standard deviations). No additional mechanism is proposed for why the dense improvement occurs; it is a direct empirical observation. The credibility for this conclusion is moderate for the same reasons as C3: the improvements are numerically consistent, but the sample size is too small to rule out chance for some of the smaller gains (e.g., 0.71-0.76 pp on ImageNet, single run). The prior probability is set to 0.55, mirroring C3.

nodes.title: Averaging Lottery Tickets subnetworks into the pre-trained dense network produces a stronger dense network

nodes.content: Subnetworks and dense networks produced by Lottery Pools exhibit improved out-of-distribution robustness: when trained on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and evaluated on their corrupted variants CIFAR-10-C/CIFAR-100-C, Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields larger accuracy gains than the original Lottery Tickets (LTs). Gains include up to 2.36 percentage points improvement for sparse ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100-C, up to 2.27 percentage points for sparse VGG-16 on CIFAR-100-C, and up to 2.38 percentage points for dense ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100-C.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 claims improved out-of-distribution robustness. The key weak point is P9: only CIFAR-C corruptions are tested, which are a single type of OoD shift. This threatens the generalization layer of the conclusion — the claim that Lottery Pools "improves OoD robustness" is implicitly about OoD in general, not just corruptions. Additionally, the statistical concerns from P2 apply to the OoD results as well (they are from the same 3-run experiments). On the credit side, H8 (standard deviations) provides some reassurance, and H6 (disagreement analysis) gives a mechanistic hint that the interpolation might broaden the effective function space, but neither highlight specifically preempts the OoD generalization risk. No highlight provides independent validation on a different OoD benchmark. The overall credibility is moderate-low: the evidence shows a clear improvement on corruptions, but the claim of "out-of-distribution robustness" is broader than what the evidence supports. The prior probability reflects that the corruption gains are likely real, but the generalization to other shift types is speculative.

nodes.title: Lottery Pools improves out-of-distribution robustness relative to original Lottery Tickets

nodes.content: In comparisons where Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) were adapted to sparse subnetworks (by pruning averaged models to the same sparsity as the original Lottery Tickets subnetworks), Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields higher test accuracy than SWA and EMA in most evaluated settings, with the advantage especially pronounced at high sparsity levels. The performance advantage is attributed to (a) per-candidate coefficient search rather than fixed averaging coefficients, and (b) the greedy candidate selection that avoids combining subnetworks from different loss basins.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 claims that Lottery Pools outperforms SWA and EMA as sparse-model combination baselines. The dominant weak point is P4: SWA and EMA use fixed, untuned coefficients, which may disadvantage them relative to Lottery Pools's searched coefficients. This threatens the comparative pattern: the observed advantage may be partially due to asymmetric tuning. H3 partially protects this by ensuring that the baselines are at least adapted to the sparsity regime (pruned to target sparsity), which preempts a more severe confound (sparsity imbalance), but does not address the coefficient tuning asymmetry. The empirical comparison across settings (Tables 8-9) shows Lottery Pools wins in most (60/76) cases, but at low sparsity the advantage diminishes. The statistical limitation P2 also applies (many wins are within 1-2 standard deviations). The overall credibility is moderate: Lottery Pools likely does outperform these fixed-coefficient baselines, but the margin may be smaller if SWA/EMA were given optimized coefficients (e.g., validation-guided search). The claim is well-supported relative to the specific baseline implementations used.

nodes.title: Lottery Pools outperforms Stochastic Weight Averaging and Exponential Moving Average for sparse subnetwork combination

nodes.content: Empirically, interpolation or averaging of Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) subnetworks yields accuracy improvements only when the subnetworks are obtained under a rewinding regime (i.e., weights are rewound to an early training point such as 5% of training); without rewinding, interpolation/averaging across IMP iterations causes substantial accuracy degradation. Thus, linear mode connectivity between subnetworks—and hence successful interpolation—depends on using rewinding.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 claims that rewinding is necessary for successful interpolation of IMP subnetworks. The primary weak point is P5: the evidence is limited to two architectures on CIFAR-100, which threatens the generalization of the "necessary" claim. P5 is partially mitigated by H6, which provides a mechanistic correlate (prediction disagreement) that connects the empirical pattern to a theoretical understanding — if rewinding is not used, SGD instability increases disagreement, making interpolation fail. H1 also directly supports the rewinding case by showing that under rewinding, linear connectivity holds across all sparsity pairs. However, no test without rewinding on a third architecture or different dataset is performed. The "necessity" claim is a strong causal statement; the evidence shows it is at least a common pattern for these architectures and this dataset. The prior probability reflects that the pattern is likely general for structured pruning under standard training, but not proven universally. The highlights (H1, H6) give the conclusion substantial credibility within the tested scope; the reservation is about the scope itself.

nodes.title: Rewinding is necessary for successful interpolation or averaging of Iterative Magnitude Pruning subnetworks

nodes.content: When combining multiple subnetworks in the greedy Lottery Pools search, applying magnitude pruning immediately after each interpolation step (prune-during) maintains robust accuracy across sparsities; by contrast, interpolating repeatedly without pruning intermediate results and pruning only at the very end (prune-after) produces dramatically worse accuracy at high sparsity. Therefore, enforcing the target sparsity (the sparsity of the original subnetwork) throughout the greedy search is empirically superior.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 8 claims that prune-during interpolation outperforms prune-after. The direct evidence is H4: a controlled ablation on ResNet-18, CIFAR-100, showing a dramatic failure of prune-after at high sparsity. This is a strong result within that setting. However, the weak point P6 notes that this is a single architecture-dataset combination without error bars. The pattern is consistent with a plausible mechanism (selection on unpruned performance fails after pruning), but without replication it is uncertain whether the pattern holds generally. No highlight provides evidence from other settings (e.g., VGG-16, ImageNet). The prior probability is moderate: the mechanism is sound and the evidence within the tested setting is clean, but the conclusion as stated ("empirically superior") implies generality. The credibility outside the tested setting is low.

nodes.title: Pruning after each interpolation step outperforms pruning only at the end in Lottery Pools

nodes.content: Empirical sensitivity analyses show that increasing the number of candidate subnetworks in $\mathcal{S}_t$ (e.g., using 4, 9, 19 candidates corresponding to 25%, 50%, 100% of possible Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) checkpoints) generally improves final accuracy; likewise, increasing the size of the candidate coefficient pool $\mathcal{S}_c$ (from a single value $\{\tfrac{1}{2}\}$ to sets of 3, 7, or 11 coefficients spanning $[0.05,0.95]$) improves performance, although gains diminish beyond moderate candidate counts.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 9 claims that larger candidate pools and more coefficients improve performance but with diminishing returns. The direct evidence is H5: a systematic sensitivity sweep on ResNet-18, CIFAR-100 showing clear diminishing returns for both factors. The weak point P7 points out that this has only been tested on one architecture-dataset pair, so the generality of the diminishing returns threshold (e.g., 9 candidates suffice) is uncertain. The direction (larger pools help) is likely general, but the specific threshold may differ. No highlight provides replication on other settings. The prior probability reflects that the qualitative pattern (diminishing returns) is robust, but the quantitative guidance should be treated as specific to CIFAR-100/ResNet-18.

nodes.title: Increasing candidate subnetwork and coefficient counts generally improves Lottery Pools with diminishing returns

nodes.content: A single subnetwork produced by Lottery Pools can attain predictive accuracy comparable to an output-space ensemble of nearby Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) subnetworks (averaging predictions across multiple subnetworks) while keeping the same inference-time memory and compute as a single subnetwork (i.e., $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cost).

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 10 claims that a single Lottery Pools subnetwork matches the predictive performance of an output ensemble while maintaining O(1) inference cost. The direct evidence is H9: a comparison to a 3-member ensemble of adjacent subnetworks on ResNet-18, CIFAR-100, showing accuracy within 0.1-0.2 pp. The weak point P8 notes that the ensemble is minimal (3 members); a larger ensemble would be stronger, so the claim of "matching ensemble performance" is relative to a specific weak ensemble. Additionally, the comparison is only on one architecture-dataset. The prior probability is moderate because it is plausible that a larger ensemble exceeds the Lottery Pools subnetwork, but the fact that weight-space interpolation can nearly match even a small prediction-space ensemble is itself a meaningful result. The conclusion as stated ("matches ensemble predictive performance") is somewhat ambiguous; if interpreted as matching the best possible ensemble from the same candidates, it is not supported. The credit from H9 is limited to the specific ensemble size used.

nodes.title: Lottery Pools matches output ensemble predictive performance with single-model inference cost

nodes.content: In the Lottery Pools procedure applied to a ResNet-18 or VGG-16 trained on CIFAR-100 (19 IMP iterations, rewinding at 9 epochs, target sparsity range from 80% to 1.8% weights remaining), the greedy search over candidate subnetworks and interpolation coefficients uses a validation set of 5,000 images (10% of the 50,000 training images) to compute ValAcc for acceptance decisions. This small validation set (5,000 images across 100 classes) is evaluated up to 209 times (19 candidates × 11 coefficient values) per target subnetwork. Repeated evaluation on a fixed, small validation set risks overfitting the search choices—the selected coefficients and candidate ordering may be optimal for this specific validation split but yield lower test accuracy on a different split.Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the validation set is not representative of the test distribution or if overfitting occurs, then the coefficient and candidate choices that maximize ValAcc will produce a final subnetwork with lower true test accuracy than the original LTs, contrary to the reported gains. The conclusion that Lottery Pools consistently improves accuracy would then be false for the specific validation split used, and the reported numerical improvements would not generalize. The entire empirical support for Conclusion 2's claim of "stronger subnetwork at fixed sparsity" depends on the validation accuracy being a reliable proxy for test accuracy across all candidates; if this link fails, the greedy search becomes a noisy optimizer that can degrade performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: The validation set is only 5,000 images, which is modest for CIFAR-100's 100 classes (50 per class). With 209 evaluations, the probability that at least one spurious high ValAcc is selected by chance is non-negligible. The paper does not report cross-validation or a hold-out test set check on a separate held-out partition, so there is no guard against overfitting. Greedy sequential selection compounds this risk because each acceptance updates the best subnetwork and the next candidate is evaluated relative to this already-selected model, inducing dependence across evaluations that can amplify overfitting.

nodes.title: Validation set overfitting risk due to small validation set in greedy search

nodes.content: For CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the test accuracy of Lottery Pools (Interpolation) and the original Lottery Tickets (LTs) is reported as the mean over 3 independent runs. Standard deviations are typically 0.1-0.4 percentage points. With only 3 runs, the 95% confidence interval for the mean difference between Lottery Pools and LTs is approximately ±1.7 × the pooled standard deviation, or roughly ±0.2-0.7 percentage points. The claimed improvements are up to 1.88 pp on CIFAR-100 (VGG-16) but are smaller at many sparsities (e.g., ~0.5-0.8 pp at 32.77% weights remaining for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100). For improvements on the order of 0.5-0.8 pp, the confidence interval spans zero, meaning the observed gain is not statistically significant at the 95% level.

metadata.failure_mode: If the true mean improvement is zero or negative, then the conclusion that Lottery Pools yields consistent in-distribution accuracy gains across architectures and datasets would be invalid for the configurations where the observed gain is not statistically significant. The claim of "up to 1.88 percentage points increase" would still be a point estimate but would not support the broader generalization that the method consistently improves accuracy. The paper's primary quantitative evidence for Conclusion 3 would be substantially weakened, and the conclusion would reduce to "Lottery Pools sometimes improves accuracy in these experiments," not a general empirical regularity.
metadata.weakness_reason: A sample size of 3 is extremely small for quantifying a population mean when the underlying distribution is unknown. The t-distribution with 2 degrees of freedom has very heavy tails, making confidence intervals wide. The paper does not report any hypothesis test (e.g., paired t-test or bootstrap confidence interval) or effect-size measure. Many of the reported gains are of a magnitude that is comparable to or smaller than the noise floor estimated from 3 runs. It is possible that the true mean improvement is zero or even negative for some configurations, and the reported positive averages are artifacts of sampling variation.

nodes.title: Limited statistical power from 3 runs for in-distribution gains

nodes.content:
On ImageNet with ResNet-18 and ResNet-34, Lottery Pools (Interpolation) accuracy and the original Lottery Tickets (LTs) accuracy are each reported from a single run; the observed improvements over original LTs range from 0.43 to 0.76 percentage points across sparsities. Typical run-to-run variation in ImageNet top-1 accuracy for standard training is on the order of 0.1-0.3 percentage points, and the Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) rewinding process introduces additional randomness. With a single run, there is no way to separate the systematic improvement from random variation.Fig. 8
      Table 10

metadata.failure_mode: If the single-run improvements on ImageNet are due to random variation, then the conclusion that Lottery Pools yields consistent ID accuracy gains across architectures and datasets would not be supported for ImageNet. The generalization of the method to large-scale datasets would be unconfirmed, weakening the broad claim of Conclusion 3. The numerical gains (0.55% on ResNet-18, 0.63% on ResNet-34) would not be reproducible, and the method might show degradation in other independent runs.
metadata.weakness_reason: A single run provides no estimate of variability. The observed improvements are small (≤0.76 pp) and within the range of possible run-to-run variation. The paper notes that ImageNet experiments were run with "limited large-scale evaluation resources" and only one run was performed. This is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation in the open questions. Without multiple runs, the numerical values cannot be used to support the claim that Lottery Pools consistently outperforms LTs on ImageNet.

nodes.title: Single-run ImageNet results lack statistical confidence

nodes.content: In the comparison between Lottery Pools and SWA/EMA for sparse subnetworks, Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) uses a uniform averaging coefficient of 1/(n+1) (averaging all checkpoints with equal weight), and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) uses a fixed decay factor of 0.95. These coefficient values are not tuned on the validation set. Lottery Pools, in contrast, searches over 11 candidate coefficients in [0.05,0.95] per candidate pair, selecting the α that maximizes validation accuracy. If the optimal averaging coefficient for achieving high accuracy after pruning to the target sparsity (the sparsity of the original Lottery Tickets subnetworks) differs from 1/(n+1) or 0.95, then SWA and EMA are evaluated at a disadvantage relative to Lottery Pools.

metadata.failure_mode: If SWA and EMA were given the same validation-guided coefficient search (or a more tailored coefficient schedule), they might achieve accuracy much closer to or exceeding Lottery Pools. In that case, the conclusion that Lottery Pools outperforms common weight-averaging baselines would be an artifact of asymmetric tuning. The attribution of the advantage to the greedy candidate selection (as the paper argues) would be incorrect; the real advantage would be the coefficient search, which could be added to SWA/EMA as well. The quantitative performance advantage reported (e.g., up to 2 pp on CIFAR-100 at high sparsity) would shrink or vanish.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's own sensitivity analysis (Fig. 5) shows that using only a single coefficient α=0.5 (Lottery Pools Average) yields lower accuracy than using multiple coefficients. SWA's uniform average corresponds to a single effective α that varies per checkpoint but lies near 0.5 for many runs; EMA's decay=0.95 is a fixed choice. These may not be the optimal coefficients for maximizing accuracy after magnitude pruning at the target sparsity. The performance gap observed between Lottery Pools and these baselines may be partly attributable to the coefficient search rather than to the candidate selection mechanism.

nodes.title: Fixed coefficient choices for SWA and EMA may disadvantage baselines

nodes.content: The claim that rewinding is necessary for successful interpolation/averaging of Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) subnetworks is based on accuracy heatmaps that compare with-rewinding and without-rewinding cases, showing a substantial accuracy drop without rewinding for all sparsity pairs. The evaluation uses a specific rewinding point (9 epochs for CIFAR-100) and specific IMP hyperparameters (20% pruning per iteration, 19 iterations). The claim that rewinding is "necessary" has not been tested on other architectures (e.g., ResNet-34, ResNet-50, transformers), other datasets (e.g., ImageNet), or with different rewinding epochs or pruning schedules.

metadata.failure_mode: If the necessity of rewinding does not generalize to other architectures (e.g., wider ResNets, ViTs) or other datasets (e.g., ImageNet with different rewinding points), then the scope of Lottery Pools would be narrower than the paper implies. The conclusion that rewinding is necessary for interpolation would be an overstatement; it would be a finding limited to VGG-16/ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 under the tested conditions. Users applying Lottery Pools to new settings where rewinding is not used might incorrectly expect failure, or conversely, if rewinding is not necessary in those settings, the conclusion would be misleading.
metadata.weakness_reason: The heatmaps show results for specific experiments; no error bars or multiple runs are reported for the heatmap values. The claim of "necessity" is a strong causal statement that would require evidence that without rewinding, no linear mode connectivity exists across a broad range of settings. The paper only shows two architectures on one dataset. Moreover, the without-rewinding case uses the same training procedure but without recording early weights; it is possible that with different learning rate schedules or longer training before interpolation, some connectivity could be restored.

nodes.title: Generality of rewinding necessity limited to tested settings

nodes.content: The ablation comparing prune-during and prune-after is performed for a single setting: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, using the full Lottery Pools greedy search with 19 candidates and 11 coefficients. The results show a single line per strategy, with no error bars. The prune-after strategy shows a dramatic accuracy drop below 10% weights remaining, while prune-during maintains stable accuracy down to 1.8% weights remaining. This particular pattern may depend on the architecture, dataset, search order, or the specific candidate pool.

metadata.failure_mode: If the prune-after strategy performs similarly to prune-during on other architectures (e.g., VGG-16, ResNet-34 on CIFAR-100, or ResNet-18 on ImageNet), then the conclusion that prune-during is empirically superior would not generalize. The design choice of always pruning after each interpolation (a core part of the Lottery Pools recipe) would be less critical, and a simpler design (interpolate all then prune) could work. The computational cost of the method could be slightly reduced. More importantly, the robustness of the conclusion at high sparsity would be undermined if the advantage is not universal.
metadata.weakness_reason: Ablation on a single dataset-architecture combination provides only limited evidence for the general superiority of prune-during. The paper does not vary the candidate pool composition, search order, or sparsity schedule to test whether the advantage holds across different configurations. Without error bars, it is unclear whether the sharp drop in prune-after is a consistent outcome or a single-run artifact. The explanation given (prune-after selects on unpruned performance which later degrades) is plausible but not directly tested.

nodes.title: Prune-during vs prune-after comparison limited to one setting

nodes.content: The sensitivity analysis for candidate subnetwork count (4, 9, 19) and coefficient count (1, 3, 7, 11) is performed on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18. The analysis shows that increasing candidate count from 4 to 9 gives a consistent improvement of ~0.2-0.5 pp, but from 9 to 19 the gain is below 0.1 pp at most sparsities. Similarly, increasing coefficient count from 3 to 7 gives modest gains, and from 7 to 11 the gains are negligible. These diminishing returns may not hold on larger datasets (e.g., ImageNet) or with deeper architectures, where more diversity across candidates could yield continued improvements with larger pools.

metadata.failure_mode: If on ImageNet or other large-scale tasks, increasing the candidate pool from 9 to 19 (or beyond) yields substantial additional gains (e.g., >0.3 pp), then the guidance that 9 candidates suffice would be incorrect for those settings. The conclusion that larger candidate pools provide diminishing returns would be an overgeneralization from limited evidence. Practitioners using Lottery Pools on different tasks might incorrectly limit their candidate pools, missing out on larger benefits.
metadata.weakness_reason: The analysis is conducted on a single dataset-architecture pair with one IMP configuration. The number of candidates (19) is determined by the number of IMP iterations, which is fixed at 19 for CIFAR experiments; the pattern might differ when more candidates are available (e.g., with more IMP iterations) or when the candidate pool contains subnetworks from different IMP runs (not just iterations). The paper does not report error bars for these sensitivity results, so the observed trends may not be statistically reliable.

nodes.title: Sensitivity analysis only on CIFAR-100, limited generalizability

nodes.content: In the comparison between Lottery Pools and output ensemble, the ensemble averages the predictions of three subnetworks: the target subnetwork and its two immediate Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) neighbors. A larger ensemble (e.g., all 19 subnetworks, or a diverse selection of distant subnetworks) would likely achieve higher accuracy, potentially exceeding the Lottery Pools subnetwork by a larger margin. The claim that Lottery Pools "matches ensemble predictive performance" is therefore relative to a minimal, three-member ensemble.

metadata.failure_mode: If a larger ensemble (e.g., all 19 subnetworks) achieves significantly higher accuracy than the three-member ensemble, then Lottery Pools would not match that ensemble's performance. The conclusion that Lottery Pools provides ensemble-like predictive performance would be incorrect for the full ensemble. Users seeking the highest possible accuracy would still prefer the ensemble, and the claim that Lottery Pools is a substitute at O(1) cost would be less compelling because the ensemble used is weaker than what is practically available.
metadata.weakness_reason: Three is a small ensemble size; the literature shows that ensemble accuracy improves with more members up to a point. The paper does not compare to the ensemble of all available candidate subnetworks. Moreover, the ensemble uses uniform averaging; weighted ensemble could be stronger. The figure shows that Lottery Pools is sometimes slightly below the ensemble's accuracy (by ~0.1 pp). The claim of "matching" is qualitative and not statistically tested.

nodes.title: Ensemble baseline used only three members, a weak comparison

nodes.content: Out-of-distribution robustness is evaluated on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C, which contain common corruptions (noise, blur, weather, digital) at five severity levels. These corruptions cover a limited set of distribution shifts. Other important OoD scenarios such as natural distribution shifts (CIFAR-10.1, CINIC-10), domain shifts (e.g., from CIFAR to SVHN), or adversarial perturbations are not tested. The robustness benefits observed on CIFAR-C may not transfer to these other shift types.

metadata.failure_mode: If on other OoD benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10.1, CINIC-10, or a domain adaptation task like CIFAR to SVHN), Lottery Pools shows no improvement or degrades relative to LTs, then the conclusion that Lottery Pools improves OoD robustness would be an overstatement. The scope of the claim would be limited to corruption-type shifts, which the paper does not explicitly acknowledge in the conclusion statement. The up-to-2.36 pp gains on CIFAR-100-C would not be representative of OoD robustness in a broader sense.
metadata.weakness_reason: CIFAR-C is a widely used OoD benchmark, but it represents only a specific family of distribution shifts. The paper claims that Lottery Pools improves OoD robustness relative to original LTs, but the evidence is limited to one type of shift. The mechanism by which interpolation improves robustness on corruptions (likely through weight averaging) may not hold for shifts that change the label distribution or input distribution in fundamentally different ways (e.g., CIFAR-10.1, which is a natural selection bias shift).

nodes.title: OoD evaluation limited to CIFAR-C corruptions only

nodes.content: Lottery Pools greedily processes candidate subnetworks in order of adjacency to the target subnetwork. At each step, if the interpolated subnetwork $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}$ (computed as $\alpha_{best} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best} + (1 - \alpha_{best})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i$, then magnitude-pruned to target sparsity, i.e., the sparsity of the original subnetwork) yields non-decreasing validation accuracy, $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ is replaced by $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}$. This sequential accumulation may cause $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ to drift away from the original target subnetwork's loss basin, potentially passing through regions where subsequent candidates become less beneficial. The ordering of candidates (by Iterative Magnitude Pruning adjacency) is not systematically justified; a different ordering might lead to a different, possibly better, final subnetwork.

metadata.failure_mode: If the greedy sequential interpolation leads to significant drift from the target basin, then the final subnetwork may have a different mask and weight configuration than what would be obtained by a global selection method (e.g., all-pairs interpolation followed by selection). The final accuracy could be lower than what is achievable with a different ordering or a non-sequential selection. In such a case, the conclusion that Lottery Pools produces a "stronger subnetwork" would still be true relative to the original LTs, but the claim that the greedy recipe is an effective way to exploit IMP byproducts would be weakened if a better approach exists that does not accumulate drift. The method's sensitivity to ordering would mean that the reported improvements are contingent on the specific adjacency order used.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides no theoretical or empirical analysis of the drift phenomenon. The greedy search is validated only end-to-end by the reported improvements, but it is not compared to alternatives (e.g., random order, reverse order, or a one-shot interpolation of all candidates with a single coefficient). The decision to accept if validation accuracy does not decrease is a local criterion that may not be globally optimal; accepting a candidate that slightly improves validation could lead to a situation where a later candidate that would have given a larger improvement is now less effective because the current best model has moved. The adjacency ordering is based on the assumption that nearby iterations share the same loss basin (supported by Fig. 1), but the effect of order on the accumulated model is not examined.

nodes.title: Sequential greedy interpolation may accumulate drift from target

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 and VGG-16 on CIFAR-100 under the rewinding regime (rewinding point = 9 epochs), the paper systematically varies the pair of IMP subnetworks by sparsity (from dense to 1.8% weights remaining) and computes the test accuracy of the averaged-then-pruned subnetwork for every pair (Fig. 1 for ResNet-18, Fig. 9 for VGG-16). The heatmap shows that for adjacent subnetworks (neighboring IMP iterations), the averaged subnetwork has higher test accuracy than either parent subnetwork at every tested sparsity. For non-adjacent pairs, the gain diminishes and eventually turns to a loss. Additionally, interpolation curves with α from 0 to 1 at increments of 0.1 (Fig. 2) show that the test loss is concave in α, with the minimum typically near the middle (α≈0.5) for adjacent pairs under rewinding. This direct, systematic evidence across the full sparsity space demonstrates that adjacent IMP subnetworks lie in the same linearly connected loss basin, providing a mechanistic foundation for why interpolation between them improves accuracy at fixed sparsity.

metadata.credit: The linear mode connectivity verification preempts the failure mode in which interpolation could destroy accuracy because the subnetworks are in different loss basins (a concern raised by prior work for models trained with different random seeds or without rewinding). By showing that for adjacent subnetworks under rewinding the linear path is a valley of low loss, the paper underwrites the core assumption of the interpolation method (Conclusion 1). The heatmap's full coverage of all sparsity pairs and three architectures (including VGG-16) rules out the possibility that connectivity holds only for a specific pair or sparsity. Without this evidence, the strong result that simple averaging works would be an unexplained empirical observation; with it, the paper provides a compelling mechanistic reason that gives substantial credit to the interpolation formula in Conclusion 1 and to the necessity of adjacency and rewinding in Conclusion 7.

nodes.title: Verification of linear mode connectivity between adjacent IMP subnetworks

nodes.content: The greedy search in Lottery Pools (Algorithm 2) processes candidate subnetworks sequentially: at each step, only the current best subnetwork $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ and the current candidate $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i$ are loaded into memory. The interpolation, pruning, and validation evaluation are performed on these two weight vectors, and the result replaces $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ if accepted. No more than two subnetworks' worth of weights (plus the validation batch) are held in memory at any time. For k candidate subnetworks (e.g., k=19 for CIFAR experiments), this reduces memory overhead from O(k) (required if all candidates are stored simultaneously) to O(1) with respect to k.

metadata.credit: This engineering design directly preempts a failure mode where the method would not scale to large candidate pools due to memory constraints. It underwrites the claim (Conclusion 2) that Lottery Pools incurs "no additional training or inference cost" relative to a single subnetwork: the training cost is the same IMP run, and the search cost is negligible in memory. If all candidates had to be kept in memory, the method would be limited to small pools or would require costly checkpointing. The sequential design is explicitly compared to less memory-friendly alternatives (e.g., learned soup), and it makes the method practical for resource-constrained settings. Without this design, the conclusion that Lottery Pools is a viable, low-cost way to reuse IMP byproducts would be less credible because memory overhead would grow linearly with the number of candidates.

nodes.title: Memory-friendly O(1) greedy search design

nodes.content: When comparing Lottery Pools to SWA and EMA (Fig. 3b, Tables 8-9), the paper applies magnitude pruning to the averaged/interpolated model from SWA/EMA after each averaging step, restoring the target sparsity (the same sparsity as the original LTs subnetwork at that sparsity level). This ensures that all methods are evaluated at identical sparsities and that the comparison isolates the effect of coefficient selection and candidate selection rather than being confounded by different effective sparsities. Without this adaptation, SWA/EMA would benefit from the higher effective capacity of a denser interpolated model, giving them an unfair advantage over Lottery Pools which always maintains target sparsity.

metadata.credit: The adaptation preempts the failure mode where the baselines would be artificially inflated because they operate at lower sparsity. By making the comparison sparsity-matched, the paper ensures that any performance advantage of Lottery Pools is due to its specific mechanisms (coefficient search, candidate selection) rather than to having more weights. This strengthens the claim (Conclusion 6) that Lottery Pools outperforms common weight-averaging baselines. If the adaptation had not been performed, the comparison would be invalid because a denser SWA/EMA model would trivially outperform a sparser Lottery Pools model. The paper's decision to adapt the baselines in the same way as its own method (prune after each interpolation step) is a notable strength for the comparative argument.

nodes.title: Fair adaptation of SWA and EMA baselines to sparse subnetworks

nodes.content: In the ablation (Fig. 6), the paper keeps the greedy search procedure fixed (same candidates, same coefficients, same order) and varies only whether magnitude pruning to the target sparsity is applied immediately after each interpolation (prune-during) or deferred until after all candidate interpolations are completed (prune-after). For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, prune-during maintains stable test accuracy within ~0.2 pp across sparsities from dense to 1.8% weights remaining, while prune-after suffers a steep decline below 10% weights remaining, dropping by over 10 pp at the most extreme sparsity. This controlled manipulation directly attributes the success of Lottery Pools at high sparsity to the practice of enforcing sparsity throughout the search.

metadata.credit: The ablation causally demonstrates the failure mode that would occur if sparsity were not maintained during the search (prune-after): the greedy search would select candidates based on unpruned accuracy, leading to poor performance after final pruning. By identifying this mechanism, the paper provides a principled reason for the design choice, rather than leaving it as an arbitrary heuristic. This directly supports Conclusion 8's claim that "prune-during outperforms prune-after." Without this ablation, a user might naively adopt prune-after to reduce computational steps, and the method would fail at high sparsity. The controlled nature of the ablation (only one variable changed) gives strong evidence for causality within this setting.

nodes.title: Controlled ablation of prune-during vs prune-after

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, the paper sweeps candidate subnetwork count (4, 9, 19, corresponding to 25%, 50%, 100% of the 19 IMP subnetworks) and coefficient count (1, 3, 7, 11) across all sparsities from dense to 1.8% weights remaining (Fig. 4, Fig. 5). The results show consistent improvement from increasing the candidate count from 4 to 9 (gains of ~0.2-0.5 pp) but minimal gain from 9 to 19 (<0.1 pp). For coefficient count, improvement from 1 to 3 is noticeable (~0.3-0.8 pp), from 3 to 7 is smaller, and from 7 to 11 is negligible (<0.05 pp). This sweep provides empirical guidance on the marginal utility of adding more candidates and coefficients.

metadata.credit: The sensitivity analysis preempts the failure mode where a user might use an impractically large candidate pool (all 19 subnetworks) and many coefficients, incurring high validation cost, without clear benefit. By showing diminishing returns, the paper gives actionable guidance (e.g., 9 candidates and 7 coefficients capture most of the gain), making the method practical. This directly supports Conclusion 9's claim of diminishing returns. Without this analysis, the method would be open to the efficiency concern that it requires evaluating all possible combinations. The factorial design across both factors (candidate count and coefficient count) is thorough and allows the user to design a suitable configuration based on their compute budget.

nodes.title: Systematic sensitivity sweep across candidate and coefficient counts

nodes.content: The paper computes the prediction disagreement (fraction of test-set labels on which the predictions differ) between every pair of IMP subnetworks across sparsities (Fig. 10) for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100. The heatmap shows that adjacent subnetworks (neighboring IMP iterations) have low disagreement (<5% discrepancy), while distant subnetworks have substantially higher disagreement (>15%). This pattern aligns with the interpolation heatmap (Fig. 1): pairs with low disagreement produce better averaged subnetworks, while pairs with high disagreement produce worse. The paper also shows (indirectly, through the contrast of with/without rewinding in Fig. 1) that without rewinding, the subnetworks have high disagreement and are not linearly connectable. The disagreement analysis thus provides a measurable correlate of interpolability.

metadata.credit: The disagreement analysis preempts the failure mode where the necessity of rewinding and the adjacency ordering would be just empirical observations without mechanistic explanation. By linking prediction disagreement to interpolation success, the paper provides a testable, interpretable factor that correlates with whether two subnetworks can be combined. This strengthens the claim of Conclusion 7 that rewinding is necessary, because without rewinding the subnetworks would be in different basins (high disagreement), and it explains why adjacency matters (adjacent subnetworks share similar predictions and thus lie in the same basin). Without this analysis, the heatmap results would still be empirical evidence, but they would lack a conceptual framework, making the conclusion less principled and harder to extend to new settings.

nodes.title: Prediction disagreement analysis provides mechanistic insight for adjacency and rewinding necessity

nodes.content: Lottery Pools (Interpolation) is evaluated on ImageNet with ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 (Fig. 8, Table 10), showing improvements over original LTs at every tested sparsity from 100% to 16.78% weights remaining. The improvements are up to 0.55 pp for ResNet-18 and up to 0.63 pp for ResNet-34. The direction and relative magnitude of improvements are consistent with the CIFAR-100 results, despite the substantially larger dataset (1.2M images, 1000 classes) and deeper architectures.

metadata.credit: These results extend the empirical support beyond CIFAR to a large-scale setting, which is where sparse models are most needed for computational savings. Even though the results are from single runs (as noted in P3), the consistency in direction across two architectures and all sparsities provides non-trivial evidence that the method transfers. Without the ImageNet experiments, the conclusion that Lottery Pools yields consistent ID accuracy gains across architectures and datasets (Conclusion 3) would be limited to relatively small-scale CIFAR benchmarks. The ImageNet results, despite their statistical limitations, are a substantive strength because they test the method in a regime where many techniques fail to scale.

nodes.title: Consistent ImageNet results across two architectures

nodes.content: All test accuracy results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (Tables 8, 9) are reported as means and standard deviations over 3 independent runs. The standard deviations are small (typically 0.1-0.4 percentage points for both Lottery Pools and original LTs), indicating that the observed improvements are consistent across runs and not driven by a single outlier. This allows the reader to assess the variability of the estimates.

metadata.credit: Reporting standard deviations preempts the failure mode where a single-run improvement could be attributed to luck. With 3 runs, the small standard errors provide some confidence that the point estimates are reliable at the scale of the measured differences. Although 3 runs are not enough for formal significance tests (as P2 notes), the presence of standard deviations is still a strength over papers that report only single runs or omit variability entirely. It supports the credibility of the claimed gains in Conclusion 3, Conclusion 4, Conclusion 5, and Conclusion 6 by showing that the positive differences are not just a single outlier.

nodes.title: Standard deviations from 3 independent runs reported for all CIFAR experiments

nodes.content: In Fig. 7, Lottery Pools (Interpolation) is compared to an output ensemble that averages the softmax predictions of three subnetworks: the target subnetwork and its two immediate IMP neighbors. The test accuracy of Lottery Pools is within 0.1-0.2 percentage points of the ensemble across all sparsities (from dense to 1.8% weights remaining) for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100. This comparison uses the same set of three subnetworks for both methods, isolating the effect of combination space (weight space vs. prediction space).

metadata.credit: This comparison directly addresses a key practical question: can a single Lottery Pools subnetwork replace an ensemble of LTs? The matched set of subnetworks ensures that any performance difference is due to the combination method, not to the quality of members. The result that Lottery Pools nearly matches the ensemble's accuracy while requiring only O(1) inference cost (single forward pass) is a strong demonstration of the method's practical value. Without this comparison, the claim that Lottery Pools provides ensemble-like performance would be unsubstantiated. Even though the ensemble is small (3 members), the match is a non-trivial finding because prediction-space combination is generally optimal; matching it with weight-space interpolation is a notable result.

nodes.title: Direct comparison to output ensemble of the same subnetworks

steps.reasoning: Start from the established empirical requirement that subnetworks must be obtained under a rewinding regime for linear interpolation between IMP subnetworks to be effective (the result established earlier: rewinding is necessary for successful interpolation/averaging between IMP subnetworks).

Introduce notation for sparse subnetworks: denote a learned sparse subnetwork parameter vector by $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$, where $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ is the dense parameter vector with zeros at positions pruned under some binary mask $m^t$ (i.e., $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=m^t\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ for mask $m^t$, dense parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ at rewinding step $j$, and elementwise product $\odot$). Define two such learned subnetworks as $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_1$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_2$.

Define the linear interpolation between two learned subnetworks: introduce the interpolation coefficient $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and form the interpolated parameter vector
$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter} = \alpha \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_1 + (1 - \alpha)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_2,
$$
which linearly mixes the two sparse parameter vectors in parameter space (this expression is explicitly given as the subnetwork created by interpolating in the authors' formulation).

Address sparsity preservation after interpolation: averaging or interpolating two sparse subnetworks can reduce the number of exact zeros (i.e., sparsity can decrease because nonzero weights from one parent may fill zeros of the other); to restore the target sparsity level the authors apply magnitude pruning to $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter}$, i.e., remove the smallest-magnitude weights from $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter}$ until the resulting vector attains the same target sparsity as the intended parent subnetwork (this magnitude-pruning-after-interpolation step is described and used throughout the method).

Treat as known the linear interpolation formulation for two learned subnetworks $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{inter}=\alpha\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_1+(1-\alpha)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_2$ and the necessity of rewinding for effective interpolation; these are starting points for the Lottery Pools construction.

Define the inputs and pools used by the Lottery Pools algorithm: let $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$ denote the target IMP-produced sparse subnetwork learned at IMP iteration $t$; define the Candidate Lottery Pool $\mathcal{S}_t=\{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t-1},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t+1},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{t+2},\dots\}$ as a set of other learned subnetworks sorted by adjacency to $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$ in IMP iteration order; define the Candidate Coefficient Pool $\mathcal{S}_c=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$ with $\alpha_j\in(0,1)$ as the discrete set of interpolation coefficients to search over.

Define the auxiliary operations and evaluation metric used in the greedy search: define the magnitude-pruning operator $\text{MagnitudePruning}(\cdot)$ which prunes the smallest-magnitude weights from a parameter vector until a specified target sparsity is reached; define the validation accuracy function $\text{ValAcc}(\cdot)$ which computes accuracy on a held-out validation set; and denote by $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ the current best candidate subnetwork during the greedy search, initialized as $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}\leftarrow\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$.

Describe the greedy interpolation-and-selection loop precisely (algorithmic recipe): iterate over each candidate $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i\in\mathcal{S}_t$ (in adjacency order), and for each candidate do (a) compute $\alpha_{best}=\arg\max_j \text{ValAcc}\big(\text{MagnitudePruning}(\alpha_j\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}+(1-\alpha_j)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i)\big)$ where $\alpha_j\in\mathcal{S}_c$ (i.e., search the candidate coefficients for the one that yields highest validation accuracy after pruning to target sparsity), (b) form $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}=\text{MagnitudePruning}\big(\alpha_{best}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}+(1-\alpha_{best})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i\big)$, and (c) replace $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ by $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter}$ only if $\text{ValAcc}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{Inter})\geq\text{ValAcc}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best})$ (i.e., accept only non-degrading interpolations). Repeat until all candidates in $\mathcal{S}_t$ are considered, yielding the final $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$.

State memory- and compute-related implementation details and cost guarantees: the authors implement a memory-friendly variant that avoids loading all candidates simultaneously by iteratively interpolating one candidate at a time and updating $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ (thus maintaining only one extra copy of interpolated weights); because the result is a single sparse subnetwork, inference cost remains that of a single model (i.e., $\mathcal{O}(1)$ relative to a single subnetwork), as summarized in the paper's method comparison. 
Table 1

Conclude the algorithmic recipe and its claimed properties: the described practical algorithm, called Lottery Pools, constructs a stronger subnetwork from an IMP-produced target subnetwork $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t$ by (1) forming $\mathcal{S}_t$, (2) defining $\mathcal{S}_c$, (3) greedily iterating over $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i\in\mathcal{S}_t$ and selecting per-candidate $\alpha_{best}$ via validation-accuracy-maximizing magnitude-pruned interpolation, and (4) updating $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{best}$ only when validation accuracy does not decrease; the procedure requires no additional network training and preserves single-model inference cost ($\mathcal{O}(1)$).

Treat the Lottery Pools algorithm (greedy interpolation of IMP subnetworks with per-candidate coefficient search and magnitude pruning to maintain target sparsity) as an established procedure (result from the previous conclusion) to be evaluated empirically across architectures and datasets.

Specify the experimental evaluation setup used to measure in-distribution (ID) test accuracy improvements: the authors evaluate on architectures VGG-16, ResNet-18, and ResNet-34 (definitions: VGG-16 and ResNet-$n$ denote the standard convolutional network architectures of those names used in the experiments), on datasets CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet; subnetworks are produced by IMP with rewinding roughly to 5% of training and the Lottery Pools (Interpolation) variant searches interpolation coefficients in the Candidate Coefficient Pool (in main experiments 11 coefficients from $0.05$ to $0.95$ are used). Implementation and training hyperparameters (e.g., epochs, batch sizes, learning rates, rewinding epochs) are reported in the paper's implementation tables.
Table 2

Present the quantitative CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 empirical results demonstrating consistent ID accuracy gains: for CIFAR-100 the authors report that Lottery Pools (Interpolation) improves over original lottery-ticket subnetworks (LTs) by up to $1.88$ percentage points with VGG-16 and up to $1.72$ percentage points with ResNet-18; for CIFAR-10 the reported gains are up to $0.93$ percentage points (VGG-16) and $1.05$ percentage points (ResNet-18). These numeric improvements are reported in the experiments and appear in the main result summaries and detailed tables.
Fig. 3(a)

Present the ImageNet empirical results demonstrating ID accuracy gains at multiple sparsity levels: in the appendix results the authors report that, on ImageNet, Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields up to $0.55$ percentage point improvement for sparse ResNet-18 and up to $0.63$ percentage point improvement for sparse ResNet-34 relative to original LTs; these ImageNet improvements are documented in the appendix figure and tables.
Fig. 8

Summarize the empirical pattern and its consistency across settings: across the reported architectures (VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34), datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet), and multiple target sparsity levels, applying Lottery Pools (Interpolation) to IMP-produced subnetworks yields consistent increases in test accuracy of the resulting sparse subnetworks, with the above-cited quantitative maxima as representative examples of the improvements observed.
Start from the Lottery Pools interpolation procedure as established (i.e., the greedy interpolation search with magnitude pruning that produces a strengthened sparse subnetwork).

Describe the alternative application of interpolation/averaging to produce a dense model: instead of producing a single sparse subnetwork as the final output, the authors apply the averaging/interpolation of learned LT subnetworks back into the pre-trained dense model parameters (that is, the weights of the original dense network are updated by averaging/interpolating the learned LT subnetworks and/or by applying the interpolation/averaging result to the dense weights); when necessary to restore sparsity constraints the authors follow with magnitude pruning to the desired sparsity, otherwise they evaluate the resulting dense network as a denser/fully dense model.

Provide the empirical CIFAR-100 dense-model improvements obtained by averaging LTs back into the pre-trained dense model: the authors report that for CIFAR-100 the resulting dense network constructed via Lottery Pools (Interpolation) exceeds the original pre-trained dense ResNet-18 accuracy by up to $2.22$ percentage points and exceeds the original dense VGG-16 by up to $1.69$ percentage points; these numerical gains are explicitly reported in the main experimental summary and result tables.
Fig. 3(a)

Provide the empirical ImageNet dense-model improvements reported in the appendix: the authors report that on ImageNet the constructed denser networks show improvements of up to $0.71$ percentage points for ResNet-18 and up to $0.76$ percentage points for ResNet-34 over the corresponding original pre-trained dense models; these results are given in the appendix figure and tables.
Fig. 8

Conclude the claim about producing a stronger dense network: averaging the set of learned LT subnetworks back into the pre-trained dense network (via the Lottery Pools interpolation/averaging procedure followed by magnitude pruning where appropriate, or by averaging and applying to the dense weights) can produce a dense network with higher accuracy than the original pre-trained dense model, as evidenced by the reported CIFAR-100 and ImageNet improvements.

Describe the out-of-distribution (OoD) evaluation protocol used to test robustness: train models (original LTs and Lottery Pools variants) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 training sets, and evaluate on the corresponding corrupted benchmark datasets CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C (where CIFAR-$n$-C denotes corrupted versions of CIFAR-$n$ with various synthetic corruptions); the held-out validation split procedure and dataset sizes used in experiments are described in the dataset details.

Present the empirical OoD gains observed for sparse and dense models: the authors report that Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields larger accuracy gains on corrupted datasets than original LTs, with reported improvements including up to $2.36$ percentage points improvement for sparse ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100-C, up to $2.27$ percentage points for sparse VGG-16 on CIFAR-100-C, and up to $2.38$ percentage points for the dense ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100-C; these gains are explicitly reported in the experiments and illustrated in the OoD figure.

State the authors' interpretation: the improved OoD robustness of subnetworks and dense networks produced by Lottery Pools is attributed to the "ensemble-like" property of interpolation — the interpolated subnetworks inherit robustness benefits analogous to those achieved by output-space ensembles, while preserving single-model inference cost.

Start from the Lottery Pools method (greedy interpolation with per-candidate coefficient search and pruning) and the presence of other weight-averaging baselines adapted to sparse settings (SWA = stochastic weight averaging, EMA = exponential moving average).

Describe how SWA and EMA are adapted for comparison in the sparse-subnetwork context: SWA averages weights of multiple checkpoints with fixed equal coefficients (or incremental averaging coefficient $1/(n+1)$ where $n$ is current model count) and EMA averages weights exponentially with a fixed decay factor (the authors set decay factor $0.95$ in experiments); for a fair comparison the authors prune the averaged/EMA models to the target subnetwork sparsity during interpolation (i.e., they apply the same magnitude-pruning step to the averaged weights so the baselines produce models at the intended sparsities).

Report the empirical comparative results showing Lottery Pools superiority: the authors show in experiments (detailed in tables and figures) that Lottery Pools (Interpolation) yields higher test accuracy than SWA and EMA in most evaluated settings, with the advantage especially pronounced at high sparsity levels; concretely, the authors report that Lottery Pools outperforms SWA and EMA in all ImageNet cases and in most CIFAR-10/100 cases (the paper states LP outperforms these baselines in most cases, with a count of wins on CIFAR-10/100 reported as 60 out of 76 evaluated cases).

Record the authors' attributed reasons for Lottery Pools' advantage: (a) SWA and EMA use pre-chosen fixed averaging coefficients/decay factors (i.e., do not search per-candidate coefficients), which may not generate interpolated subnetworks that maximize validation accuracy at the target sparsity, whereas Lottery Pools searches for an optimal coefficient per candidate; (b) Lottery Pools' greedy candidate selection can avoid combining subnetworks that lie in different loss basins (i.e., it prevents averaging across models from different basins), reducing destructive interference from incompatible combinations.

Conclude the comparative claim: therefore, when SWA and EMA are adapted to sparse subnetworks by pruning averaged models to the target sparsity, the Lottery Pools interpolation procedure yields higher test accuracy than SWA and EMA in most evaluated settings, especially at high sparsity, with the performance advantage attributed to per-candidate coefficient search and greedy candidate selection that avoids mixing different loss basins.

Define the iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) procedure and the rewinding regime used to obtain lottery-ticket subnetworks: let $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ denote the dense network parameters; let $m^t$ denote a binary mask at pruning iteration $t$ that zeros out pruned parameters; the IMP loop consists of (a) saving the weights at $j$ training steps as $\boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ (where $j$ denotes the rewinding point), (b) at each pruning iteration pruning the lowest-magnitude fraction $p$ of weights and updating the mask $m^t$, and (c) training the masked network $m^t \odot \boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ to completion. Here $j=0$ corresponds to rewinding to initialization and $j>0$ corresponds to rewinding to an early training point; in the experiments reported the authors use rewinding to roughly the 5% training time (i.e., $j$ corresponding to 5% of the full training schedule).

Report the empirical comparison between averaging/interpolating subnetworks obtained with rewinding versus without rewinding: the authors present an accuracy heat map that shows, for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, that when subnetworks are obtained under the rewinding regime, averaging/interpolating two nearby IMP subnetworks tends to produce averaged subnetworks with higher test accuracy than the original parent subnetworks at the same sparsity; conversely, when subnetworks are obtained without rewinding, averaging/interpolating across IMP iterations produces a significant accuracy drop across all sparsities.
