Connect the empirical observation to the concept of linear mode connectivity and prior findings: the authors note that the observed dependence of successful weight interpolation on rewinding aligns with previous work showing that sparse subnetworks discovered by lottery-ticket procedures are only linearly connected (stable to SGD perturbations) when obtained under rewinding; thus linear interpolation between subnetworks (i.e., existence of a linear path of low loss/low error between them) is present only in the rewinding regime. The prior reference for the instability without rewinding is the work that introduced the rewinding concept and linear mode connectivity for lottery tickets.

Conclude the necessary empirical condition: therefore, interpolation or averaging of IMP subnetworks yields accuracy improvements only when the subnetworks are obtained under a rewinding regime (i.e., weights are rewound to an early training point such as 5% of training); without rewinding, interpolation/averaging across IMP iterations causes substantial accuracy degradation, implying that linear mode connectivity between subnetworks—and hence successful interpolation—depends on using rewinding.

Start from the Lottery Pools greedy interpolation procedure and the operational choice of when to apply magnitude pruning during multi-candidate interpolation: define "prune-during" as applying magnitude pruning immediately after each interpolation step within the greedy search (i.e., after forming each interpolated vector the smallest-magnitude weights are removed to restore target sparsity before evaluating and possibly accepting the interpolation), and define "prune-after" as postponing magnitude pruning until after all greedy interpolations are completed (i.e., perform pruning only once at the end).

Describe the empirical comparison performed by the authors: the authors compare prune-during and prune-after across multiple sparsity levels and report the resulting test accuracies in a dedicated figure; the experimental setup uses the same greedy interpolation and candidate pools, differing only in the timing of applied magnitude pruning.
Fig. 6

Report the empirical outcome and observed trend: the authors find that prune-after (i.e., delaying pruning until the end) causes dramatic accuracy degradation at high sparsity levels, whereas prune-during (i.e., pruning after every interpolation step) maintains steady high accuracy across all sparsities; the figure shows prune-after's accuracy dropping sharply in the high-sparsity regime while prune-during remains robust.

Record the authors' explanation for the observed difference: in prune-after the greedy search selects interpolated networks based on un-pruned performance (i.e., performance before enforcing the target sparsity), which can favor interpolations that look good un-pruned but perform poorly at the target sparsity after final pruning; in prune-during the greedy search always evaluates candidate interpolations at the desired target sparsity (because pruning is applied immediately), ensuring that selected interpolations are effective at the target sparsity throughout the search.

Conclude the empirical superiority statement: therefore, when combining multiple subnetworks in the greedy Lottery Pools search, applying magnitude pruning immediately after each interpolation step (prune-during) maintains robust accuracy across sparsities, while interpolating repeatedly without pruning intermediate results and pruning only at the very end (prune-after) produces dramatically worse accuracy at high sparsity; enforcing target sparsity throughout the greedy search is empirically superior.

open_questions.content: The work leaves several explicitly acknowledged and practically important unresolved issues. First, learning optimal interpolation coefficients and selecting subnetworks via gradient-based or joint optimization (rather than the proposed greedy, validation-guided search) was noted as possible but computationally expensive; whether such optimization yields further gains at reasonable cost remains unresolved. Second, the paper reports limited large-scale evaluation resources (ImageNet experiments were run with fewer repetitions and constrained compute), so establishing statistical significance, evaluating variability across multiple independent runs on ImageNet and on substantially larger modern architectures, and characterizing scaling behavior remain open empirical tasks. Third, while the experiments show that rewinding is necessary for successful interpolation and that adjacency in IMP iteration correlates with interpolation success, a precise theoretical characterization of when two IMP subnetworks are linearly mode-connected (and thus interpolable without loss) — including the role of SGD noise, rewinding point, and prediction diversity — is not resolved by this work and is left as an open scientific question.
